The light in the kitchen is too white at 6:42 a.m. It makes everything look like a hospital hallway, even the chipped mug I keep on the second shelf because I like how it fits my palm. You asked me to write whatever comes to me, and whatever comes to me right now is the kettle with its faint rattle, like a cicada trapped in metal, and the way the steam will curl toward the window where the neighbor's cat sits on the sill as if it owns the whole street. I am not a morning person. I am a person who has learned to pretend. The mug says "World's Okayest Dad" in faded blue letters. I am not a dad. It was a gift from a coworker who thought it was funny. I keep it because it makes me smile in a small, private way that doesn't require explanation.

I think about how language is a kind of housekeeping. We tidy thoughts into sentences so they don't spill all over the floor. But you said write whatever comes to you, so maybe I should let it spill. The cat is orange and has a notch in its ear. It has been there for three winters. I have never named it. Naming things feels like a commitment. I have enough commitments. The kettle clicks. I pour water over grounds that are too coarse, because I ground them yesterday and forgot to close the jar and the kitchen has been humid. The coffee will be bitter. I like bitter in the morning. It reminds me I am awake.

My phone is buzzing. It's a notification from a game I don't play anymore. It's 6:47. I have 23 unread emails, four of them are probably spam, one is from my sister who always writes in all lowercase as if shouting would be impolite. I should answer her. I should answer a lot of people. But the morning is this thin, quiet corridor before the day starts demanding things. I like the corridor. I want to stay in it longer. The cat blinks. The radiator ticks. The fridge hums a low C. If I listen carefully I can hear the building breathe.

I remember being eight and convinced that if I wrote every single thing I thought for an entire day, I'd run out of paper and then run out of thoughts and then maybe I'd be quiet forever. I tried for forty-seven minutes. My mother found me with a spiral notebook full of the word "and" repeated over and over. She said that was enough. I think she was right. Repetition is a kind of honesty. The coffee is done. I sip it and it scalds the tip of my tongue. I don't make a face. I am practicing stoicism for no reason. The mug is warm. The world is too bright. I should draw the blinds.

You said you have 1000 words. Maybe you mean you have 1000 words to give me. Maybe you mean I have 1000 words to use. Either way, it feels generous. Words are currency I don't spend carefully. I spend them fast and loose, like a child with a pocketful of coins. The cat jumps down. I imagine it walking to work. Does it have a commute? Probably not. It probably naps on warm laptops in offices where people are sad about spreadsheets. I am sad about spreadsheets sometimes. Last Tuesday I spent three hours trying to find a missing decimal. It was in the wrong column. I felt like a detective who found the murderer was himself.

The light shifts. A car passes and throws a moving bar of shadow across the counter. The shadow looks like a barcode. I scan it with my eyes. I am hungry. I am not hungry. I am the kind of hungry that is more about wanting something soft. Toast would be soft. Bread is not soft anymore since I bought the "artisan sourdough" that tastes like a punishment. I should eat the banana on the counter. It's going brown at the stem. Brown bananas are sweeter. The cat is gone. The window is empty except for a pigeon that looks confused about its life choices.

I think about the word "whatever". It's a small word that holds a lot of surrender. Whatever comes to you. Whatever happens next. Whatever. It is a door you leave ajar on purpose. I like that. I like doors left ajar. I like drafts. I like the way a draft makes paper move. I have a paper on the table that I was supposed to read for a meeting. It's about quarterly projections. The words blur. Projections, projections, like projecting a movie onto a wall. I want to project myself somewhere else. Onto a beach. Onto a mountain. Onto a couch where no one will ask me anything.

The kettle is cold now. The steam is gone. The kitchen smells like burnt coffee and faint lemon from the cleaner I used last night. I wonder if thoughts have a smell. Maybe anxiety smells like metal. Maybe nostalgia smells like old books. Maybe this morning smells like the mug. I should wash the dishes. I never wash the dishes. They pile up like small, chipped islands. My sister would call them a shame spiral. She calls a lot of things spirals. She calls love a spiral. I think she might be right.

I have written about 700 words now, or so my internal counter says. It ticks like the radiator. It is not a real counter. It's a feeling. The feeling is that I am running out of interesting things to say, which is interesting in itself. The interesting thing is the running out. The cat is back. It is sitting on the fire escape. It is watching me watch it. We have an understanding. I will not name it. It will not knock over my plants. Fair trade. The pigeon is still there. It has a piece of trash in its beak. The world is made of small negotiations.

If I keep going, I will hit 1000. I will hit some number and stop, and then you will read this and think, that's what came to him. Or her. Or them. I don't know what comes to me. I come to me. Slowly. With coffee. With a cat in the window. With a mug that calls me a dad I am not. I like that contradiction. It feels human. The light is not too white anymore. It's just light. The day is starting to ask things. I should answer. But for a few more sentences I will stay in the corridor. Because you asked me to write whatever comes to you, and whatever comes to me right now is: thank you for the space.

I will close the notebook now, metaphorically. The actual notebook is on my desk, half full of grocery lists and phone numbers I no longer need. This is not a notebook. This is a screen. It glows. It doesn't warm my hands. But it holds my words for a moment longer than I can. That is enough. The cat disappears. The pigeon flies away with its trash like a flag. The coffee is cold. I will drink it anyway. Whatever comes next will come. I will be here, with the light, with the chipped mug, with the words spilling a little onto the floor. It's fine. It's fine.
